newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends higher, sets 34-mth high vs mark in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends higher, sets 34-mth high vs mark in U.S.

text.p: The dollar closed firmer, and hit a new 34-month high against the mark aided by confidence in the relatively strong U.S. economy and hints the Bundesbank has few objections to the dollar's rise, dealers said.

The dollar hurdled 1.7050 marks, its previous 1997 high, in early European trade, buoyed by strong U.S. economic data on Monday, and talk that Germany's jobless rate may have surged to another post-war high in February.
The unit received another lift in early U.S. dealings after the release of strong U.S. housing market data, they said.

The dollar eventually touched 1.7162 marks, its highest since late April 1994, after Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm said the dollar's recent advance was an "appropriate" correction from its record low in 1995 and that this view does not change with movements of just a few pfennigs.

"Im sure the market is thinking: 'Well, how does 1.75 (marks) grab you?' That is the comment (Palm's) that got everybody's interest," said Stephen Jury, chief foreign exchange dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland, in New York.
The dollar ended at 1.7132/37 marks on Tuesday, up from 1.7090/93 at the open.
The dollar also rose to 122.10/15 yen from 121.85/90 and to 1.4860/70 Swiss francs from 1.4830/37 Swiss.
The market shrugged off other remarks by Palm who also said postponing the planned 1999 launch of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be dangerous.
These remarks were drowned in a deluge of comments from various Bundesbank officials which did little to clarify market concerns regarding possible delays to EMU.
The 8.6 percent leap in January U.S. new single-family home sales reported on Tuesday, compounded the belief a vibrant economy might lead to higher U.S. interest rates.

The data came on the heels of strong U.S. construction spending and healthy wage and personal consumption data released on Monday, and indicates that dollar-denominated financial instruments could become more attractive compared to mark-based investments, traders said.

"I think the underlying elements of the economy that support the strong housing market are important when you talk about relative growth," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International.
Moreover, the weak German economy almost ensures the Bundesbank will not raise interest rates soon, experts said.

The market is on heightened alert for higher U.S. interest rates after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan told a Senate panel last Wednesday that the Fed could tighten credit even before solid signs of inflation emerge.
Meanwhile foreign exchange market operators mostly ignored Greenspan's comments to the Budget Committee of the House of Representatives on Tuesday.

Economists and traders are waiting for Wednesday, when the Fed chief completes his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the House Banking Committee, expecting a replay of his performance last week.

"We're poised to raise rates here," said James Powers, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York. "Greenspan said that obviously last week -- a possible preemptive rate hike, etcetera and the economy chugging along well. The U.S. looks like a pretty good place to be in."
Elsewhere, the dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3693/98 from C$1.3695/00 at the open. The pound fell to $1.6135/45 from $1.6160/70. The Australian dollar eased to $0.7882/87 from $0.7890/00.
